d.title: The four letters, and what actually enforces each
d.caption: Only one of the four is free. Atomicity and durability are the engine's own machinery; consistency is whatever constraints you declared, and isolation is a level you chose — usually the default, which permits more than most people expect (6.2).

d.title: An idempotent load: the pipeline's version of atomicity
d.caption: A pipeline that is re-run after a failure must not double-count. Wrapping the delete and the insert in one transaction makes the re-run safe: either the partition is replaced or nothing changed, and no reader ever sees the gap between the two.

items.label: BEGIN
items.desc: nothing is visible to anyone else yet

items.label: DELETE FROM target WHERE day = :day
items.desc: removes whatever a previous run left

items.label: INSERT INTO target SELECT ... WHERE day = :day
items.desc: writes this run's rows

items.label: COMMIT
items.desc: both become visible at the same instant

items.label: Re-run it
items.desc: the same day's rows are replaced, not added again

d.title: Five anomalies against three isolation levels
d.caption: READ COMMITTED — the default on PostgreSQL and SQL Server — permits four of the five. That is not a bug: the levels are a contract about what the engine will prevent, and anything it does not prevent is yours to prevent with a lock, an atomic write or a constraint.

d.title: Three fixes that work at any isolation level
d.caption: Each removes the read-modify-write gap rather than asking the engine to police it. The third is the one to reach for first, because a single statement cannot interleave with itself.
cells: nothing: no gap to interleave in

d.title: What an upsert actually does
d.caption: `ON CONFLICT` needs a unique constraint to conflict *against* — without one there is nothing to detect, and the statement inserts a duplicate. `EXCLUDED` is the row that was proposed, which is how the update reaches the new values.

items.desc: the proposed row

items.label: ON CONFLICT (key)
items.desc: needs a UNIQUE or PRIMARY KEY on that column

items.label: DO UPDATE SET col = EXCLUDED.col
items.desc: EXCLUDED is the row that was proposed

items.label: DO NOTHING
items.desc: the other choice: keep what is already there

items.label: RETURNING *
items.desc: tells you which rows were written

d.title: Five constraints, five refusals
d.caption: Every rule left to the application is a rule the database will eventually see broken, because some other writer will not have read your code. NOT NULL is the cheapest and the most valuable: a column that can be NULL will be, and every query on it then needs a COALESCE branch.

d.title: A surrogate key and a natural one
d.caption: They are not alternatives: use a surrogate as the primary key so that a business identifier can change without cascading updates through every child table, and declare the natural key UNIQUE so the database still enforces what makes a row real.

columns.title: Surrogate: a serial or UUID
items: Narrow: cheap in every child table

d.title: The schema for taking orders is wrong for analysing them
d.caption: One shape makes each write touch a single place; the other makes each question touch few tables. They are different objectives, and trying to serve both from one schema is how a reporting query ends up joining eleven tables.

columns.title: Operational (OLTP)
items: Writes touch one row in one place
A report joins a dozen tables

columns.title: Analytical (OLAP)
items: One wide fact table, a few dimensions
A report joins two or three tables

d.title: Slowly changing dimensions: what happens when a tier changes
d.caption: The choice decides what a historical report says. Type 1 rewrites history — every past order is relabelled, which is exactly the leak of 7.2. Type 2 keeps a row per version with validity dates, which is what an as-of join needs.

d.title: Which schema changes are cheap and which lock the table
d.caption: The cost is decided by whether existing rows must be rewritten or verified. Adding a nullable column is a catalogue edit; adding a NOT NULL column with no default has to touch every row, and on a large table under load that is an outage.

NOT VALID defers it, then VALIDATE

d.title: Expand and contract: a breaking change in safe steps
d.caption: The rule is that the schema and the application are never required to deploy together. Each step leaves both the old and the new code working, so any step can be rolled back on its own.

items.desc: old code ignores it; nothing breaks

items.label: Write to both
items.desc: deploy code that fills old and new

items.label: Backfill in batches
items.desc: old rows get the new value, a chunk at a time

items.label: Read from the new one
items.desc: deploy; the old column is now unread

items.label: Contract: stop writing, then drop
items.desc: two deploys apart, so a rollback is possible

d.title: The differences that produce a wrong answer, not an error
d.caption: Dialect differences that raise a syntax error are harmless — you fix them immediately. These are the ones that run and return something plausible on the other engine, which is why portable code writes the explicit form every time.

d.title: Row, column, embedded
d.caption: The storage layout decides what the engine is good at, and it is not a matter of maturity. A row store fetches a whole record in one page read; a column store reads one column of a billion rows without touching the others.

d.title: The f-string and the parameter
d.caption: A parameter is not an escaping function — the value never becomes part of the statement's text. The engine parses the query once, with a placeholder where the value goes, so there is no string for an input to break out of.

columns.title: f"... WHERE name = '{name}'"

d.title: What a parameter cannot be
d.caption: A placeholder stands where a *value* goes. Anything the parser needs in order to understand the statement cannot be a parameter — and that is the point at which people reach back for string formatting, so these are the places to validate against an allow-list.
cells: this is what placeholders are for

d.title: The leak: Asha was standard in January
d.caption: The customers table holds only the current value, so joining it onto orders labels every January order `plus` — a feature that did not exist when the order was placed. For a model predicting refunds or churn it quietly encodes 'this customer stayed long enough to upgrade', which is the future leaking into the past.

d.caption: All three answer 'what was true at the moment of this row'. The first is the one to reach for: a validity range on the dimension turns the as-of join into an ordinary inequality join the planner understands.

d.title: Cohorts, funnels and RFM are the same three moves
d.caption: Four of the analyses a product team asks for are one pattern with different anchors. Naming the three moves is what makes the fourth request a ten-minute query rather than a new puzzle.

items.label: Define the entity's anchor moment
items.desc: signup month, first purchase, the funnel's entry event

items.label: Bucket time relative to the anchor
items.desc: months since signup, steps since entry, days since last order

items.desc: retention is a share, not a count

items.label: The funnel adds one rule
items.desc: each step must happen after the one before it, per entity

d.title: Why a funnel needs the order enforced
d.caption: Counting people who did each step independently is not a funnel: someone who checked out and then browsed again counts in both, and the 'conversion' includes paths that never happened. The fix is a timestamp comparison per entity, which is what LAG or an as-of join gives you.

d.title: A hash split and ORDER BY random()
d.caption: A hash of the key is deterministic: the same row lands in the same fold today, tomorrow and on another machine, and a new row joins a fold without moving any existing one. `random()` gives a different split on every run, which makes a result impossible to reproduce.

columns.title: MOD(ABS(HASH(id)), 10)
items: The same row, the same fold, always
No sort: it is one expression per row
New rows do not move old ones

columns.title: ORDER BY random() LIMIT n
items: Sorts the whole table to take n
A seed helps, and is easy to forget

d.title: The split that leaks
d.caption: A random row-level split puts rows of the same entity, or the same moment, on both sides — and the model then scores well by recognising something it has already seen. The grain of the split must match the grain the prediction is made at.

cells.text: both sides hold the same person

d.title: The dozen questions, and what each one is really testing
d.caption: Every interview draws from the same small set, and each is a concept in a costume. Naming the concept out loud — 'this is a ties question, so DENSE_RANK' — is most of the answer, and it is what the follow-up question is aimed at.

d.title: How to talk through one
d.caption: The code is the smallest part of the answer. What is being assessed is whether you state the grain, name the edge case before it is pointed out, and say what you would check — which is the same discipline the rest of this course has been about.

items.label: Say the grain of the answer
items.desc: one row per what: per customer, per customer-month

items.label: Name the edge case first
items.desc: ties, NULLs, customers with no orders, months with none

items.label: Write the simplest version
items.desc: a CTE per step, named, rather than one nested block

items.label: Say how you would check it
items.desc: a row count you can predict, a spot-check on one key

items.label: Offer the scale caveat
items.desc: what you would change at a billion rows, and why
